item.title: China urges Japan to accelerate destruction of abandoned chemical weapons
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 08:07:00
This photo taken on Nov. 25, 2026 shows the scene of a side event hosted by the Chinese delegation at the 31st Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CSP-31) in The Hague, the Netherlands. China urged Japan to accelerate the destruction of abandoned chemical weapons in China at the CSP-31 in The Hague on Wednesday, stressing that prolonged delays in addressing the issue remain a major practical obstacle to achieving "a world free of chemical weapons." (Xinhua/Shao Haijun) China urged Japan to accelerate the destruction of abandoned chemical weapons in China at the 31st Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CSP-31) in The Hague on Wednesday, stressing that prolonged delays in addressing the issue remain a major practical obstacle to achieving "a world free of chemical weapons." The Chinese delegation hosted a side event titled "Current Status and Challenges with Respect to the Destruction of the Chemical Weapons Abandoned by Japan on the Territory of China," highlighting delays in the destruction process and calling on Japan to fulfill its obligations under the Convention. More than 100 representatives from over 40 countries attended the event. According to the Chinese delegation, Japan has missed its deadlines for destroying the abandoned chemical weapons four times. The latest plan, adopted in 2022, is due to expire in 2027, putting Japan at risk of missing the deadline for a fifth time. Japan's budget for addressing the abandoned chemical weapons in China was cut by 22 percent this year compared with 2025, even as its defense budget continued to rise. Shen Bo of China's Permanent Representation to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) said discussions at the Conference of the States Parties had reflected several shared understandings within the international community regarding the Japanese abandoned chemical weapons. "Concerns are growing over delays in the destruction process, particularly the risk that Japan could miss the 2027 deadline. The international community expects Japan, as the state that abandoned the weapons, to fulfill its obligations under the Convention and accelerate their destruction," Shen said. He said Japan must adopt a serious and responsible attitude toward its historical, political and legal responsibilities. Any attempt to whitewash its wartime crimes or rewrite history would not be accepted by China or the international community. "Japan must show genuine commitment by faithfully fulfilling its obligations under the Convention and substantially increasing investment in personnel, technology and funding. It must also take swift action by providing accurate information on burial sites, improving the efficiency of excavation and recovery operations, and assuming responsibility for treating contaminated soil and water," Shen told Xinhua after the side event. Vladimir Tarabrin of the Permanent Representation of the Russian Federation to the OPCW said Russia's position on the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan during World War II was "clear and unequivocal." "This is not a matter of Japan's goodwill, nor is it an act of charity. It is Japan's legal and moral obligation to rid itself of this legacy of the Second World War as soon as possible," he added. OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior stressed that recovering and destroying the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan in China is an important part of the international community's shared goal of permanently and completely eliminating chemical weapons worldwide. "This is a difficult task, but one that must be accomplished," she said.

item.title: Beijing turns recyclables into public seats, eyeing circular economy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 08:06:00
A visitor learns about waste plastic recycling process during the 2024 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at the China National Convention Center in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 14, 2024. (Xinhua/Wu Qinghao) Since the start of the year, Beijing has installed 48 eco-friendly benches made from recycled materials across 26 public spaces, as part of the capital's efforts to promote waste sorting and build a circular economy. The public spaces span historic streets, city parks, waterfront greenways and commercial plazas in seven districts, namely Dongcheng, Xicheng, Chaoyang, Haidian, Fengtai, Shijingshan and Tongzhou, the Beijing Municipal Commission of Urban Management said. The recycled seats come in two main types. The "cloud benches" are made from polypropylene materials such as recycled takeout boxes and plastic drink cups, which go through washing, shredding, modification and injection molding. Each contains material recycled from roughly 1,000 takeout containers. The "board benches" are made from milk cartons that are sorted, stripped of their aluminum and plastic layers, and crushed before being hot-pressed into recycled composite board. Each recycled seat features a sign explaining where its recycled materials came from and how much was used. Beijing has been expanding its recyclables collection system in recent years, linking neighborhood drop-off points, transfer stations and sorting centers so that low-value recyclables such as plastic takeout boxes and drink cups can be collected, transported and processed. This takeout-container recycling network now covers more than 20 universities, parks and railway stations, over 140 office buildings and 11,207 communities with recycling machines. The capital has also launched a citywide online recycling platform that lets residents book door-to-door pickup for old furniture, renovation waste and used appliances, and publishes prices for recyclables such as paper, plastic, metal and textiles. "What matters in building a full recycling chain is not making end products into showpieces, but giving residents feedback when they sort and letting them see the results in public spaces, so that sorting continues to be turned into resources," said Liu Jie, an official with the Beijing Municipal Commission of Urban Management. According to the commission, Beijing will add more recycled benches in more places, including upgraded neighborhoods, improved parks and commercial areas with better walking and cycling routes, while continuing to strengthen its recyclables collection system.

item.title: China and EU avoided the worst outcome, but much more needs to be done: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 00:01:00
China EU Photo:VCG This is not the best possible outcome, but it is a pragmatic arrangement that has avoided the worst. The so-called "import quotas" essentially impose restrictions on foreign automakers' exports through compulsory measures. They are inherently protectionist to some extent and, in a broader sense, create uncertainty for the global automotive supply chain. On November 24, the European Commission announced the adoption of import quota restrictions on hybrid vehicles from China and other regions, with the provisional measures set to last for 200 days. China's quota stands at 192,000 vehicles, equivalent to an annual quota of 350,000, higher than that allocated to any other source of imports. On the same day, China's Ministry of Commerce responded by urging Brussels to "earnestly abide by the consensus between the two sides." From the EU's initial proposal to the release of this preliminary ruling, the process involved more than 30 rounds of consultations. The negotiations were arduous, and the outcome was hard-won. This is not the best possible outcome, but it is a pragmatic arrangement that has avoided the worst. The so-called "import quotas" essentially impose restrictions on foreign automakers' exports through compulsory measures. They are inherently protectionist to some extent and, in a broader sense, create uncertainty for the global automotive supply chain. Previously, many voices argued that the introduction of the so-called "import quotas" was specifically aimed at China. This "flawed achievement" represents a pragmatic balance reached by both sides against the broader backdrop of China-EU relations. The EU initially based its calculations on the average import volume over nearly three years, proposing an annual quota of only around 70,000 hybrid vehicles for China, while Japan would have been allocated 257,000 vehicles over the same period. The EU also at one point demanded that China impose so-called "voluntary export restrictions," a request China rejected in accordance with the law and relevant rules. Upholding the three principles of "respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules," China insisted that the issue be addressed within the framework of the WTO. In the end, China secured a higher quota based on the actual import volume of 302,000 vehicles in 2025. For a provisional measure lasting just 200 days and still at the preliminary ruling stage, the fact that the process did not descend into an escalation of confrontation is already a "second-best solution" under the circumstances. China and the EU are key trading partners to each other, and differences between them are only natural. What is abnormal is treating ordinary industrial competition as a contest over status and resorting to walls and restrictions to ease insecurity. The tortuous consultation process once again demonstrates that, as long as both sides adhere to the principles of mutual respect and equal-footed consultations and address issues within the framework of WTO rules, ways can always be found to manage differences. From the 16 specific point consensus reached at the second meeting of the consultation mechanism in October to the finalization of the latest arrangement on hybrid vehicles, repeated practice has shown that China and the EU have the capacity to transcend differences and achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes. Hopefully the EU will earnestly honor the consensus reached by both sides, strictly abide by WTO rules, fully implement the principle of non-discrimination, and conduct relevant investigations in a fair and impartial manner. It is worth noting that trade barriers that should never have existed in the first place reveal Europe's barely concealed industrial anxiety. It is precisely this mounting anxiety that is driving the EU into an increasingly defensive posture, erecting barriers first against battery electric vehicles and then against hybrid vehicles. Faced with the decline of Europe's automotive industry, rather than seeking ways to provide financial support and encourage traditional automakers to innovate and transform, the EU is resorting to tariffs and quotas to buy time for domestic automakers to navigate their transition. Meanwhile, sustained geopolitical engagement and commitments have driven up energy and raw material prices, further increasing the pressure on European automakers to stay afloat. Europe is currently pressing ahead with its green transition in the hope of enhancing its competitiveness, while simultaneously fearing "overdependence" on Chinese green and environmentally friendly products. This reflects a deeply conflicted mindset. In reality, far from driving Europe's traditional automotive industry into a corner as the European side claims, China's new energy vehicles have instead opened up entirely new opportunities. In October this year, German automaker Volkswagen's NEV deliveries in China rose to 4.5 times the level recorded in the same period last year, reaching a record 28,000 units. Deliveries of its ID.AURA T6 model exceeded 12,000 units, making it the best-selling model in the midsize NEV SUV segment. This is a prime example of European automakers proactively integrating into China's industrial and supply chains and achieving market success. Similar success stories abound in other industries. Protectionism offers no way forward; openness and cooperation are the right path. China's recent signing of a protocol with Switzerland to upgrade their free trade agreement and its extension of mutual tariff exemptions with Canada demonstrate the value of dialogue and mutually beneficial cooperation. Europe needs to shake itself out of its self-induced complacency. Hopefully the European side will meet China halfway, provide industries on both sides with a stable, predictable and sustainable environment for trade and investment, and promote the stable, balanced and sound development of bilateral economic and trade relations. China will also closely monitor the progress of the EU's subsequent investigation and reserves all rights, including recourse to dispute settlement and seeking trade compensation under the WTO framework, to resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of the relevant Chinese industries. There is no fundamental conflict of interests between China and Europe, whose industries have complementary strengths and are deeply integrated. A confident, autonomous and open Europe would not only serve the common interests of China and Europe but also enable Europe to find its rightful place amid the sweeping global changes unseen in a century.

item.title: Media coverage of Australia-Solomon security deal full of geopolitical calculations
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 23:21:00
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (R) speaks during a joint press conference with Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale after signing the Australia-Solomon Islands Treaty at Parliament House in Canberra, Australia, November 25, 2026. Photo: VCG Australia and Solomon Islands signed a security treaty on Wednesday. One day earlier, Australian media had already floated the claim that the Pacific Island Country's (PIC) security pact with China, which will expire in April 2027, is not to be renewed. The way Australian media and other Western media outlets reported the Australia-Solomon pact is worth a closer look. Australia's ABC News, citing a Lowy Institute analyst, described the pact as a "massive win" for Australia. US media such as Politico and British media such as Reuters and the Guardian called it "a blow" for China's ambitions in the Pacific. The asymmetry in vocabulary is itself part of the media "script." Unpack it, and the pattern becomes unmistakable: The words routinely applied to Australia are "partnership," "reassurance," "deepening ties," each of which presupposes legitimacy and reciprocity, while applied to China, the cooperation is encoded as "grip," "foothold," "expansion," each term presupposing erosion and threat. Reading between the lines of such scripts, one cannot help but sense a kind of mean-spirited triumph. When Australia-Solomon cooperation is framed, marketed and celebrated primarily as a means of excluding China, the tell is in the language: The deal is a "massive win" only if someone else has lost; it is newsworthy chiefly as "a blow" to an imaginary rival. The satisfaction that accompanies each "blow" to China and each "win" for Australia is not the satisfaction of a genuine diplomatic achievement, but one of seeing a rival's legitimate presence delegitimized. For a long time, Australia and Western countries have treated China as a hypothetical adversary in the South Pacific. This framing is not incidental - it is the organizing principle behind much of their commentary on the region. When China provides aid and investment to PICs, or engages in normal cooperation with them, these activities are systematically tagged with geopolitical labels. Development assistance is recast as strategic penetration; infrastructure financing is recast as debt leverage; routine diplomatic engagement is recast as interference. The vocabulary shifts, but the function remains the same: to ensure that any Chinese presence in the Pacific is read through the lens of threat rather than through the lens of what it actually delivers. Each claim against China, however thinly sourced, reinforces a broader picture in which China's regional role is inherently illegitimate. The reporting is not aimed at establishing facts; it is aimed at establishing a consensus. And that consensus serves a clear geopolitical agenda: preserving the strategic primacy that Australia and its Western partners have long assumed in the South Pacific. Zhen Feiyang, a research fellow at the Center for Economic Diplomacy, Wuhan University, told the Global Times that since 2025, Australia has accelerated its push for security cooperation arrangements with PICs, including Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Fiji, attempting to build a regional security cooperation network centered on Australia that resembles the US "hub-and-spokes" system in the Asia-Pacific and assertively dominating the regional security order. The cost of this geopolitical agenda, however, is that it locks the entire region into a script of great-power confrontation. Australia and the West could celebrate the "massive win," but what they have lost is the possibility of making the South Pacific a place of genuine cooperation rather than rivalry. Their dream of primacy, too, becomes a casualty - a hegemony that can only be sustained by scripting every Pacific partnership as a contest with China is not a stable order but a permanent state of suspicion, one that exhausts the very influence they seek to preserve. As China stated, "There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and PICs, including Solomon Islands." The statement is a reminder of what the Australian and Western media's script leaves out and why the geopolitical calculations are never really about the Pacific at all.

item.title: GT Voice: India should guard against US attempts to sow discord with China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 22:48:00
India Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The US is again invoking India to advance its own agenda against China. On Tuesday, the Business Standard claimed in a headline: "China leveraging India's supply-chain dependence to curb its rise: US panel." The report cited claims by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), which alleged that China is using economic pressure, supply-chain dependencies and its support for Pakistan to constrain India's rise. Dressed up as a warning to India, the USCC report's allegations are in fact an attempt to disguise its deliberate attacks on China as being in India's national interest. It casts China's role in regional supply chains as a threat, portrays mutually beneficial economic ties between China and India as a security risk, and encourages India to view its economic engagement with China through the lens of US strategic competition. But why should India allow its own economic interests to be subordinated to America's strategic agenda? The USCC has a long record of ideological bias against China, leaving its reports with little credibility. Indian readers need not take its allegations too seriously. The question is why the commission is so intent on portraying China as a threat to India's economic development and casting bilateral cooperation in such a negative light. The report itself may offer a clue. In its executive summary, the commission claimed that "Washington and New Delhi have spent a quarter century building closer ties across defense, technology, and trade, but India will continue to guard its strategic autonomy rather than align automatically with US objectives." This may be precisely the problem the commission seeks to address. By portraying China as a threat to India's rise, the report seeks to play up US-China competition and draw India closer to the US position on China. Its allegations about China's intentions toward India should therefore be viewed in light of the commission's strategic agenda and ideological bias against China. There is a more practical way to look at India's economic engagement with China. From April to October, India's exports to China grew by 37.71 percent year-on-year. That figure deserves attention not merely as a measure of export growth, but as a reminder that China is a market offering Indian businesses growing opportunities to expand. Exports have become an important driver of India's economic growth and manufacturing expansion. China is playing an increasingly important part in that story. As India's manufacturing sector develops, the complementarity between the two countries' industrial supply chains is growing, not diminishing. The rise in India's exports to China is one sign of this. Disrupting these mutually beneficial supply-chain links would ultimately come at a cost to India's own economy. The Business Standard report refers repeatedly to China's export controls. This may reflect a concern in Indian public debate. There is, however, a broader context to consider. As China's exports become more technologically advanced and encompass a wider range of dual-use items, applying controls to specific sensitive products in line with established international practice is a normal part of a country's responsibility to uphold international security and meet its nonproliferation obligations. They should not be conflated with restrictions on ordinary trade or mistaken for an obstacle to India's manufacturing development. It is precisely at such times that some Western voices seek to sow discord between the two countries. India has good cause to be alert to such attempts. These voices may have little interest in whether India's economy and manufacturing sector develop smoothly, and may instead be guided by other strategic considerations. India has every reason to assess such arguments with a clear head and make its own judgments. India is right to continue guarding its strategic autonomy rather than aligning automatically with US objectives. The same principle applies to its economic engagement with China. India's trade and industrial interests are for itself to judge, not questions to be settled by the USCC's strategic calculations. A more constructive course is to let China-India economic cooperation grow where it serves both sides.

item.title: AI face blending makes it harder to trace unauthorized use, expert warns
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 22:33:00
Photo: VCG A short video featuring a character who bears a striking resemblance to Chinese actor Peng Yuchang, in both appearance and voice, has recently sparked online discussions about AI face-blending technology. Peng's studio has also issued a statement alleging that his facial features have been used without authorization in AI training and face-blending content and calling on those responsible to stop infringement. "AI face blending is a form of generative deep synthesis, and its technical approach is fundamentally different from that of replacement-based face swapping," Yang Jinwei, head of the AI Authenticity Verification Department at Beijing RealAI Intelligent Technology Co, told the media. In traditional AI face swapping, the process begins with a source face and a target face. Facial landmarks are aligned and the poses normalized, after which the source face's texture is mapped onto and rendered over the target person's head. Essentially, it is a process of replacement, with a clearly identifiable source image, according to Capital News, a news platform operated by the Beijing Daily Group. Face blending, by contrast, relies on a facial feature encoder to convert faces into high-dimensional latent vectors. These vectors encode identity-related information, including facial contours, the arrangement of facial features, the distance between the eyebrows and eyes, nose and lip characteristics, skin tone and texture, and habitual expressions. The system then combines multiple facial vectors through weighted interpolation and feature blending before feeding them into a diffusion model or generative adversarial network to render an entirely new face image, according to Capital News. "Creators can either import multiple face images and adjust the weights assigned to different features, or use text prompts and parameter settings to define characteristics such as face shape, facial features, age and expression," Yang said. "Some creators of infringing content seek to retain enough resemblance for viewers to recognize the public figure being imitated, while altering facial details to evade automated detection tools that platforms use to compare images against original photos," he noted. Lower technical barriers have also reduced the cost of using other people's facial and vocal features without permission. Feng Anrong, a screenwriter, director and head of an AI production team, told the Global Times that some producers of low-cost, high-volume short dramas seek to maximize profits through unauthorized AI face swapping and voice cloning. "Many low-cost, high-volume productions essentially operate like commercial in-feed advertisements, relying on unauthorized AI face blending and voice cloning to reduce production costs," Feng said. "Such productions are often made in bulk and promoted by paying for increased traffic. Rather than relying on the revenue-sharing model used by traditional short-drama platforms, they may therefore fall outside conventional content review mechanisms." The large-scale production and distribution of such content also pose challenges for platforms seeking to identify and remove infringing material. Zhang Peng, a cultural studies researcher at Nanjing Normal University, told the Global Times that such content may evade some basic automated detection systems, but this does not mean it cannot be identified or that it leaves no traces. "AI technology has lowered the cost and technical barriers to replicating people's facial and vocal characteristics. Meanwhile, technical limitations in platform moderation and the high costs individuals face when pursuing legal remedies make it difficult to promptly curb infringing content," Zhang said. "For platforms, detection needs to move beyond simply comparing images and also examine facial features, the origins of generated content and whether the necessary authorization was obtained." Zhang suggested that platforms improve the traceability of AI-generated content through measures such as digital watermarking, content-tracing technologies and databases of authorized uses, while also strengthening content moderation and complaint-handling mechanisms. As AI-generated appearances do not need to be an exact match for the people being imitated, determining whether a person's rights have been infringed has become an important issue in legal practice. Li Yunkai, an intellectual property lawyer at the Beijing Tian Yuan Law Firm, told the Global Times that the key to determining whether an AI-generated image infringes a person's portrait rights is not whether it looks exactly like the individual, but whether ordinary members of the public can identify the person. "Comments under videos and discussions on social media platforms may also serve as reference points when assessing whether an individual is identifiable," Li said. "If generated content places an identifiable person in vulgar scenarios, falsely portrays them as endorsing a product, or associates them with negative stories, it may also infringe their reputation rights, and those distributing the content may bear corresponding liability."

item.title: A growing number of older adults in China are returning to university for formal degrees, reclaiming long-deferred dreams on their own terms
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 22:06:00
Jiang Nüwu holds up her admission letter and poses for a photo in front of Northeast Normal University in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province, in 2026. Photo: Courtesy of Jiang Editor's Note: With China's population of seniors over 60 surpassing 300 million, ensuring a happy and fulfilling life for all seniors has become a pressing issue for both families and the nation. How can the new generation of seniors in China break away from traditional norms and embrace a different lifestyle, supported by AI technology, multiculturalism and an elder-friendly society? The series "Old Age, New Trends" explores emerging trends in the silver economy, creative social norms among senior citizens and innovative eldercare services. It examines the opportunities and challenges presented by an aging society, highlighting the diverse lifestyles of seniors and the booming eldercare industry in China. Beneath these new trends lies a reflection of Chinese modernization, which aims to provide more secure systems and dignified lives for its senior population. When 55-year-old Jiang Nüwu finally walked into a postgraduate classroom this autumn, just two months after retiring, she found herself surrounded by classmates mostly in their 20s and 30s. She was initially nervous. But when her class instructor introduced her to the class as an example of perseverance, her younger classmates broke into applause. The gesture put her at ease. Her return to university comes at a time when China is seeking to broaden educational opportunities for its ageing population. At a press conference in November, a National Development and Reform Commission official said authorities would implement the national plan for services for the elderly and young children, while expanding channels for elderly education and incorporating new technologies into learning programs to help the elderly bridge the digital divide. Yet for some older learners, the classroom they seek is not necessarily one designed specifically for their age group. Rather than signing up for courses in calligraphy, music or dancing at a senior university, they are taking entrance examinations, pursuing academic degrees and studying alongside younger generations. Their choices are still far from the norm among older Chinese people. But the stories have attracted growing attention on social media, where younger users have expressed admiration and even a desire to follow a similar path after retirement. Behind this interest is a changing understanding of what later life can offer. Dreams postponed, not abandoned For Jiang, being admitted to university to study a part-time master's program was the realization of a dream she had carried for around 30 years. After graduating from Jilin University, she once considered pursuing further studies in education at Northeast Normal University. But coming from a financially disadvantaged family in the mountains, she gave up on her dream. In the years that followed, she took on various jobs, including working as a cashier and a tutor. Her return to academic life was, in an unexpected way, inspired by her daughter. When her daughter began preparing for the postgraduate entrance examination while holding down a job, Jiang wanted to support her through the experience. "I suddenly had the idea of taking the exam alongside my daughter, to encourage her," she told the Global Times. Both were not confident about passing the entrance exam. While helping care for her mother, Jiang was also occupied with farm work at her mother's home. Following stomach surgery in November 2025, she used a little over a month of recovery time to review mathematics, English, logic and writing, often watching lectures at double speed. "I really value this hard-earned time to study," Jiang said. Jiang and her brother have been looking after their mother. Meanwhile, she has been working toward completing the degree in the shortest possible time. She also plans to explore psychology, a subject she enjoys, through additional courses. For 56-year-old Zhang Jiling, the decision to return to education was driven by a different kind of unfinished business. Born in Taiyuan, North China's Shanxi Province, Zhang spent much of her life doing physically demanding and informal work, including housecleaning, childcare and hairdressing. Education, however, had always been central to how she saw herself. As a young woman, she failed the annual college entrance exam, or gaokao, three times. Severe headaches that had begun during junior middle school, combined with financial pressure and diminishing family confidence, eventually forced her to abandon the pursuit. After her son entered university in 2019, Zhang began to reconsider her own educational ambitions. She took the gaokao in 2020, missing the admission threshold by just three points, then tried again in 2021. This time, she gained admission to Shanxi Technology and Business University, where she studied preschool education. "I may not have the same memory as younger people, but I believe my understanding and practical abilities can be stronger," she told the Global Times. In 2025, she graduated as an outstanding student. At the graduation ceremony, she also managed to secure an impromptu speaking opportunity, telling the graduating students: "Anyone with a dream is remarkable, and with courage, miracles are possible." After graduation, Zhang has not stopped learning. She now spends time memorizing English texts and exercising, seeing continued self-improvement as part of her everyday life. Similar stories have emerged elsewhere in China. In Central China's Hubei Province, 56-year-old Zhu Chunfang, a retired engineering professor who had spent decades working in water conservancy, took the gaokao again, earning admission to a college to study traditional Chinese medicine, the Hubei Daily reported in September. In South China's Guangdong Province, 56-year-old Li Weixin retired in August and, the following month, was accepted into a digital economy master's program. Having worked in financial management for 36 years, she wanted to rebuild her knowledge in the age of artificial intelligence. The phenomenon has also extended beyond China's borders, with an increasing number of older Chinese adults choosing to pursue academic degrees abroad after retirement. For instance, Wang Xiaoxi received an offer from the University of Athens at the age of 56, one year after retirement, to study ancient Greek archaeology, history, and literature. Elderly students take a selfie with a humanoid robot at a community service center in Hohhot, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, on November 25, 2026. Photo: VCG A seat among younger peers These stories do not suggest that large numbers of older people are abandoning senior universities or rushing back into formal education. Rather, they point to a more diverse set of aspirations emerging among some older adults, for whom retirement can mean an opportunity to revisit choices that earlier circumstances had put beyond reach, Chu Zhaohui, a research fellow at the National Institute of Education Sciences, told the Global Times. The distinction between formal higher education and senior universities is central to understanding why some older people choose the former, Chu said. Chu said that traditional senior education programs had often been designed around an assumption that retirement meant a transition toward leisure. Courses in painting, calligraphy, singing and similar activities have served important purposes, but this approach does not necessarily reflect the full range of aspirations among today's older learners, Chu said. Some want more systematic academic learning and opportunities to interact with younger generations. Even the introduction of AI and digital technology courses at senior universities may not fully address these demands. The content, teaching methods and broader learning environment can differ considerably between institutions. For some older people, the appeal of a regular university lies not simply in what is taught, but also in the company of younger classmates and the atmosphere of a conventional campus, the expert said. Stories of older people returning to university have struck a chord with some young social media users, who see the choice as an appealing vision of life after retirement. Wang Long, a 26-year-old employee at an internet company in Beijing, is one of them. Some of their experience reminded Wang of the pressures of corporate life: meetings, weekly reports and performance targets. Watching someone who had spent decades in the professional world choose an entirely new academic direction felt, in her words, like someone was finally giving working people a reason to look forward to life beyond their careers. Wang hopes to study philosophy or sociology after retirement. For now, however, she believes she cannot afford to do so. Leaving her job for a postgraduate program would mean sacrificing her income and taking on considerable tuition and living expenses. "Retirement could change that calculation. With a pension, savings and grown-up children, education could become a form of consumption rather than an investment," Wang told the Global Times. 'Keep learning for as long as I live' How open are China's regular universities to people who have already reached retirement age? According to Chu, the current mainstream admissions framework for regular higher education does not impose a blanket upper age limit. In principle, older people can enter the system through the relevant entrance examinations, provided they meet the academic requirements. In practice, examination scores remain the main hurdle. While admission to highly selective universities may be difficult for older applicants, local and less selective institutions can offer more realistic opportunities. The expert also believes that changing demographics could create new opportunities for universities. Opening more programs to older learners could offer institutions another source of demand and support their long-term development, he said. However, expanding access is not simply a matter of removing age restrictions. The circumstances of older students can differ considerably from those of their younger classmates, and their ability to pursue education often depends on factors beyond academic performance. Family responsibilities are one such constraint. Financial security is another consideration. For universities, the challenge will also be to develop arrangements that accommodate different stages of life without lowering academic standards. Flexible timetables, part-time programs and concentrated teaching schedules could help some older students balance education with family responsibilities. Questions surrounding student services, campus accommodation and the integration of students from widely different age groups will also require attention as universities explore broader participation, according to the expert. Ultimately, Chu said, the choice need not be between senior universities and conventional higher education. Recreational courses, community-based learning, digital skills programs and formal academic degrees can serve different people at different stages of life. What matters is whether older adults have meaningful opportunities to choose the kind of education they want, rather than having their needs defined solely by their age. For Jiang, returning to university has already opened up new possibilities beyond the degree itself. She hopes to continue studying psychology, improve her English and eventually write a memoir about her life. She also has a message for younger people who see retirement as a time when their ambitions can still grow. "Even with a 60-year-old body, being in that kind of environment can give you the heartbeat of a 20-year-old," she said. "As long as I am healthy, I will keep learning for as long as I live." Zhu Xuanlin contributed to this story.

item.title: China sets up BCI standardization working group amid commercialization push
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 21:51:00
A medical worker uses a brain imaging device to assess a patient's brain activity at a hospital in Bengbu, east China's Anhui Province, July 17, 2026. Bengbu, a traditional industrial city, has stepped up the development of its brain-computer interface (BCI) industry in recent years. By strengthening collaboration among industry, research institutes and medical institutions, Bengbu has built an innovation ecosystem that supports both BCI research and clinical application, aiming to become an emerging BCI innovation hub in the Yangtze River Delta region. Photo: Xinhua China has taken a significant step by advancing efforts to standardize the technology that connects human minds to computers. According to a report by chinanews.com.cn, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) announced the establishment of a new working group under its brain-computer interface (BCI) standardization technical committee at an industry conference on Wednesday. According to the MIIT, the working group has eight sub-teams covering general standards, hardware, software, data, product systems, applications, safety governance and the medical sector. This structure is designed to span the full BCI value chain, from research and development to commercial deployment, and it includes members from universities, research institutes, companies and hospitals, said the report. Industry observers said that the move reflects China's effort to pair government-led standard setting with industrialization, as leading neurotechnology companies such as Neuralink are accelerating global competition in this field. They said that standards are seen as a crucial bridge between laboratory innovation and large-scale application. According to the ministry, the working committee's general group will focus on common technical principles, typical technology models and universal testing and evaluation standards. The hardware group will work on standards for neural signal acquisition, signal preprocessing and output interfaces. The applications group will target use cases in industrial, consumer, transportation and education settings, developing standards for scenario release, deployment and adaptation testing. At Wednesday's event, organizers also released an evaluation report on BCI decoding algorithms, a key component of the BCI system, aimed at making performance testing more comparable across the industry. Sun Cong, vice president of the Wuhan Yiruide Medical Equipment New Technology Co, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the evaluation report helps solve one of the industry's biggest bottlenecks: comparability. "Different companies have used different datasets and metrics, so a 90 percent accuracy rate and an 85 percent accuracy rate could not really be compared," Sun said. "Hospitals and regulators had no way to judge which figure was more credible. This report standardizes the four steps of data preparation, algorithm testing, performance calculation and result analysis, and validates them through motor-imagery tasks. It is like giving decoding algorithms a unified ruler." He added that the new evaluation framework could serve as a basis for procurement, regulatory review and reimbursement decisions, helping high-quality products stand out while curbing exaggerated performance claims. In the first half of 2026, the BCI sector showed accelerating momentum across all segments, from product registration and clinical trials to production capacity building, the Xinhua News Agency reported. In a recent development, a team led by the School of Computer Science at Zhejiang University announced an invasive BCI system called DeepAxtiv for precision treatment of treatment-resistant depression, according to the official WeChat account of the university on Tuesday. The team said that it had conducted six prospective clinical trials in patients with severe treatment-resistant depression. Early results also showed significantly better efficacy than the current average international level, according to the university. According to industry experts, China's BCI industry is moving beyond single laboratory demonstrations toward high-throughput data collection, real-time decoding, closed-loop interaction and real-world applications, with the supply chain expanding into device engineering, system integration and product transformation. Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology showed that the number of BCI companies worldwide has risen from about 800 last year to 1,175 in 2026. In China, more than 77 percent of related companies are concentrated in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.

item.title: Taiwan island fans' invitation to 'Pursuit of Jade' stars to visit the region highlights growing enthusiasm for cross-Straits youth exchanges: Taiwan Affairs Office
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 12:31:00
Zhang's still in Pursuit of Jade Photo: Courtesy of Douban When asked to comment on the enthusiastic invitation from fans on the island of Taiwan for the two lead actors of Pursuit of Jade , a Chinese mainland costume drama popular in Taiwan region, to visit the island for exchanges, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office said on Wednesday that this was the most vivid demonstration of young people on both sides across the Taiwan Straits reaching out to one another. Zhang Linghe and Tian Xiwei, the lead actors of Pursuit of Jade , recently took part in an online fan meeting for audiences on both sides of the Straits. Many Taiwan local fans enthusiastically expressed their strong desire to invite the two actors to visit the island for exchanges. Both Zhang and Tian said they were eager to visit the island to explore its landscape, experience local life and taste the local delicacies. Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday that they have noted the reports, including discussions at the fan meeting about traditional Chinese culture, such as shadow puppetry, Qinqiang opera, flower hairpin adornments and traditional Chinese medicine. Zhang Linghe wrote a calligraphy piece reading "united through drama, together for our shared land," while Tian recalled her university-era visit to the island of Taiwan. Many fans in Taiwan voiced hopes of meeting the two actors in person and looked forward to them visiting soon, according to the spokesperson. "I believe this is the most vivid demonstration of young people on both sides across the Taiwan Straits reaching out to one another. Emotional and cultural resonance serve as a natural bond that brings people across the Straits closer together," Zhang Han said. "We welcome mainland cultural and artistic professionals to engage with audiences on the island and support cross-Straits cooperation in film and television production to create more outstanding works together," Zhang Han added. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' deliberate efforts to obstruct cross-Straits exchanges run counter to public opinion and lack public support, the spokesperson said. Zhang Linghe was previously denied permission to hold an in-person fan meeting in Taiwan region, with the Taiwan's so-called Mainland Affairs Council citing his alleged "demeaning" remarks about the island's status and insufficient details about the event's nature and purpose, the Xinhua News Agency reported.
